item.title: Opening up Attention: A QK Transcoder Dashboard for Feature Pairs
item.description:
Multi Head Attention in Transformers continues to be an elusive topic in mechanistic interpretability. One way of trying to decompose MHA into interpretable parts is applying SDL (Sparse Dictionary Learning) methods to the attention mechanism. However, despite the progress that has been made, we still don't have a firm grasp on attention patterns and their formation.

Additionally, there is an absence of comprehensive dashboard views for the attention mechanism and features present therein. Feature vis offers a tool to visualize and investigate features present in the residual stream and in the MLP, but neglect the attention mechanism.

To try to shed light on why/how attention patterns form and to visualize features that answer these questions, I introduce a query-key transcoder dashboard to be able to easily find and investigate monosemantic features in MHA.

The query-key transcoder architecture resembles Wynroe and Sharkey’s bilinear sparse dictionary learning approach. The primary contribution of this post is an interactive feature-pair dashboard for every layer/head in GPT-2 small (similar in spirit to Anthropic's SAE dashboard, but dedicated to query-key feature pairs), and an exploratory investigation using it. This is meant to be an interim, independent research report for investigating and visualizing the QK circuit of GPT-2.


Replacing dense queries and keys with sparse features

A sparse autoencoder learns to express a sparse set of features for models' internal activations. Transcoders work similarly, however instead of their reconstruction target being the same input activations, the output is the activations after some LLM transformation (usually MLP blocks, but in this case it's the query and key blocks). Specifically, the query-key transcoder acts as a replacement for the QK computation. They are two separate transcoders; the query transcoder learns a sparse set of features for every token and the key transcoder does the same. In practice L0 (the number of features active per token) ranges from about 10-20 features. Generally, earlier layer transcoders have L0 on the small side of this range and later layers require more features to reconstruct the attention pattern.

The 2 encoders read the LayerNormed residual stream vector, the query side encoder learns the query features an the key side the key features:

The transcoders each have 3-dimensional decoders of shape F × 12 × 64. This way, every feature has a decoder vector for each head:

One key characteristic of this architecture is feature activations are shared across all heads in a given attention layer. The three-dimensional decoder does not assign each feature to exactly one head. A feature can write to every head, and each head's decoder vector determines how much a particular feature contributes to the reconstructed attention pattern for that head.

The transcoder learns by replicating GPT 2's attention patterns and the original queries and keys are likewise used in the auxiliary training losses, as described below


The Loss Function

The main training signal from the loss function is Ljoint; the KL divergence between the original attention pattern and the reconstructed attention pattern. The reconstructed attention pattern is obtained by multiplying the query decoder activations with the key decoder activations, softmaxing, and dividing by sqrt(d_head).

The mixed loss sum of LQ and LK represents the auxiliary training losses. One problem with only having Ljoint is the query and key decoders can compensate for one another. To circumvent this issue, you implement a loss function with the original key and reconstructed query as well as the reconstructed key and original query to against the original attention pattern to ensure that both learned queries and keys remain faithful to the underlying model.

The last two terms in the loss function represent the sparsity and ghost gradients respectively. Sparsity penalizes too many features activating and maintains a low L0. Ghost gradients temporarily revive features that have been dead for too long and provide a learning signal in the direction of reconstruction error. This is the key architectural difference between my transcoder implementation and the bilinear sparse dictionary learning approach by Wynroe and Sharkey’s bilinear sparse dictionary learning approach. They cite that 80%-95% of features die without using any neuron resampling, whereas using ghost gradients to resample dead neurons, only 4%-12% of features die out.

ws(t) and wg(t) are the warmup functions. Since a warmup learning rate is implemented it also makes sense to scale the sparsity and ghost gradient functions by this same warmup to have cohesion between the scaled learning rates.


Interpreting the QK Feature Pair Dashboard

A layer-11 dashboard view, for an induction feature pair. Prompt: “I always loved visiting Aunt Sally. Whenever I was feeling sad, Aunt”. The selected edge is Aunt→ Sally in head 9.

1) Prompt and Token Selection

Simply choose a prompt and choose which token is the destination, and which to attend to. You can choose the layer/head you want to analyze. Top X refers to how many features present in the transcoders should be part of the analysis, it doesn't exclude the rest of the features from reconstruction, it only excludes them from the dashboard display. Top X is kept based on magnitude of feature activation.

2) Where does this destination attend?

This illustrates GPT-2's attention pattern and the reconstructed attention pattern for a given destination-source token pair. 'Selected pair's contribution across sources' determines how positively or negatively a feature pair contributes to all possible sources. The 'full causal attention map' portrays a grid-like view for both GPT-2's attention pattern and the reconstructed attention pattern.

3) Active Features at Selected Tokens

This is where you select a feature pair of interest. Oftentimes large feature activations are correlated with features that contribute highly to the attention pattern, but this is not always the case. The heatmap in the next step provides the computation behind how much a particular feature pair contributes to a specific attention pattern.

The query panel shows feature activations at the selected destination; the key panel shows them at the selected source. “L0” is the number of nonzero features at that token.

4) Query x Key Interactions

For a particular cell in the heatmap, the number shown represents the contribution made by that feature pair to the selected source-destination score. Before softmax, each source token and destination token pair has a total contribution by every feature pair and bias terms. The 'Exact decomposition of the selected source's score' shows each of this contributions.

How is a Feature Pair Computed?

To compute a feature pair, first define a compatibility score as the alignment between the query decoder direction and the key decoder direction for a particular head, h and feature pair i, j:


This is a fixed compatibility score. It says whether the two decoder directions align, oppose one another, or barely interact in this head. It can be positive or negative.

For a particular destination and source, the pair contributes:

This is the crux of the dashboard heatmap. It represents how closely the two features' decoder directions align as well as the magnitude of the features' activations.

For any source-destination token pair, each query feature can interact with each key feature. Although sparse activations reduce the number of relevant terms, 20 active query features and 20 active key features can still result in 400 pair terms. The heatmap offers a convenient method to distill the total number of pair terms down to the ones that contribute most to the attention pattern.

'Absolute coverage' simply refers to what percentage of total feature pair contribution is covered in the heatmap. For instance, 80% coverage means that the pairs displayed in the heatmap represent 80% of the sum of all the absolute pair terms, not including biases.

Centered Score vs Raw Score

The centered score view subtracts the pair’s average contribution across the legal sources:

S consists of the sources that the destination t can refer to with respect to the feature pair i, j. Centering asks whether this pair gives the chosen source a score that is higher or lower than the average score of the sources.

5) Selected Pair and Ablations

This panel is useful for ablating a feature pair and identifying how important a particular feature pair is to the reconstructed attention pattern. The panel shows the magnitude of query and key feature activation, the compatibility score, and raw contribution score to the source-destination token pair before softmax.

What exactly does “ablate the pair” mean?

For the default pair ablation, subtract that pair’s raw score contribution at every legal source in the selected destination row, then apply softmax again:

The dashboard shows the original reconstructed probability subtracted by the ablated probability; if the result is positive then removing the pair has decreased the attention given to this source whereas if it is negative then the removal has increased that attention.

The other controls answer different questions:

·        Pair, selected edge only: eliminate the term of this pair at the specified source.

·        Query feature: at the destination, remove the selected query feature, together with its interactions involving all the reconstructed key features and the key bias.

·        Key feature: remove the selected key feature at the selected source, along with its interactions with all reconstructed query features and the query bias.

We can assess how useful a particular feature pair really is in reconstructing the attention pattern by removing the pair and then recalculating the attention. In order to check whether a pair helps a destination to attend to an earlier place name, you can see if removing it leads to a reduction in attention for that place, measure how much the change is, and find out where the probability goes instead. This makes ablation a helpful heuristic for testing interpretations, rather than blindly trusting high scores on the heatmap.

6. Look for the pair in other contexts

See other contexts where the feature pair also activated. Use this section to validate hypotheses.

7. Check the reconstruction

The diagnostics include KL divergence in pattern error, total variation distance, 'Top 1 source agrees', and score decomposition error.

Total variation distance or TV is given by:

For one attention row, TV = 0.04 means four percentage points of probability mass have to be redistributed to make the two distributions match. A small value is reassuring, but can still conceal a large relative error on a particular source, so this metric is not a direct substitute for manually inspecting the reconstructed attention pattern and ensuring fidelity. 'Top 1 source agrees' simply refers to whether the reconstructed attention pattern correctly placed the majority of attention mass onto the source that should be attended to the most. And score decomposition error checks whether the feature-pair explanation adds back up to the transcoder’s actual attention scores.


Case Study

Consider these two unfinished sentences:

a) Earlier, Maya washed the rice in Rome. Later, she wanted to

b) Earlier, Maya washed the rice in Rome. Later, she travelled to

The final token is identical, the previous sentence is also identical, but the subsequent part makes either an action or a place relevant

Can we examine an attention head and see if it makes that kind of distinction?

The feature pair Q1031 and K1195 involves earlier action cues

So what?:

If you were to only inspect the attention pattern on layer 9 head 6 of GPT-2, you would see the attention mass on the attended token change from 'washed' to 'Rome', but there is no clear picture for why this change occurred. By attributing a single feature pair to source-destination pair 'to->washed' and one to 'to->Rome', we identify candidate vector directions in the query activation space and key activation space that 'cause' this change.

Note: HeadVis also provides feature-level QK attribution; however, this dashboard adopts a different method. It learns separate dictionaries of queries and keys in order to reconstruct the attention patterns, and combines the pairwise contributions along with the reconstruction diagnostics and ablations.


Limitations & Future Work

  • A label is a hypothesis. Features may combine a number of behaviors, some appear to be monosemantic but many are polysemantic. In certain cases, clear examples can cause a general lexical cue that is polysemantic to appear as if it were a precise semantic concept.
  • Features are unlabelled. I have yet to apply autointerp to the features in the transcoders.
  • These ablations establish dependence inside the reconstruction, not GPT-2 itself. To make stronger claims about GPT-2, interventions in the original GPT-2 are needed, including downstream predictions, DLA, and vector steering, to test whether the mechanisms suggested by the reconstruction are genuinely causal. Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions is especially relevant: this too looks at attention formation, using the residual-stream features and producing attribution graphs by means of the model's original QK computation.
  • QK is only part of attention. The QK circuit is only half the picture, the other half is the OV circuit. The next focus of this research direction will be to apply transcoders to the OV circuit of GPT-2 small to couple the 'which sources should be attended to given a destination' with 'what information moves from source to destination'. A dashboard that covers both these bases should provide a more cohesive picture of MHA.
  • The layers are separate models. The dashboard represents a separate query-key transcoder for each of the 12 layers. Thus, superposition across layers of attention cannot be decomposed within the transcoders.


Related work

The architecture behind the transcoder setup and training regime comes from Decomposing the QK Circuit with Bilinear Sparse Dictionary Learning. The primary way transcoders has been used in the past is based on Transcoders Enable Fine-Grained Interpretable Circuit Analysis for Language Models which uses sparse replacements (transcoders) to find interpretable decompositions in MLP blocks. With regard to attention, the work Progress on Attention looks at a number of methods for interpreting attention, one of which is QK diagonalization. The techniques described in Tracing Attention Computation Through Feature Interactions allow feature paths, which are routed according to the original attention computation, to be traced through the model. The main difference between a query-key transcoder and this research is that Anthropic's implementation obtains the residual-stream features by means of weakly causal crosscoders, while my approach involves learning separate feature dictionaries for the query and the key specifically in order to reconstruct attention patterns. This means that training is encouraged to focus on the information that is useful for forming attention patterns, whereas in the case of residual-stream reconstruction the target is more general. The dashboard is inspired by the ARENA SAE interpretability notebook.



All WandB training runs from qk transcoders trained on layers 0-11 of GPT-2.

item.title: Greater good arguments in AI safety
item.description:
Back in the before-time of the 2010s, when EA was still known mostly for funding health efforts in the developing world, there were many baskets of criticism floating around from the left. The most prominent was a cluster centered around EAs being white men, and therefore suspicious.[1] Another category, in my experience the second-most common, was that in attempting to rectify the problems in the world, EA was masking, whitewashing, and misdirecting efforts away from solving the "real problem", usually capitalism but often other contradictory forces.

These arguments were often not specific to EA, but mainstream arguments against charitable giving in general. On any Hacker News post about a billionaire giving to charity, one of the first few comments would inevitably be this Oscar Wilde quote:

Just as the worst slave-owners were those who were kind to their slaves, and so prevented the horror of the system being realized by those who suffered from it, and understood by those who contemplated it, so, in the present state of things in England, the people who do most harm are the people who try to do most good.[2]

These arguments have a long history. Anticapitalist critiques of charity go back to Engels and Marx, who called charitable givers a bourgeois faction intent on "redressing social grievances in order to secure the continued existence of bourgeois society." In their most explicit form these critiques had the following shape:

  • There is a "root cause" of most societal ills, such as capitalism.
  • Billionaires giving to deworming efforts addresses the symptoms of this problem, such as poverty and disease. But it's not treating the root cause.
  • Additionally, a side effect of such giving is that it gives people reason to tolerate the current system better, or even begin to like their oppressors, which gets in the way of fomenting change.
  • So actually, deworming people in Africa, or giving legal aid to poor people in the U.S., is net-negative. You should just spend all of your time trying to change capitalism.[3]

While you could argue with these proposals on the object level, I think most people have an intuitive sense that this line of thinking is fraught, independent of whatever political program is mentioned. One general concern you might have is that if you're going to claim that the first-order effects of someone's good work are swamped by some second-order effect, particularly some second-order effect on optics, then the burden of proof is pretty high. And clearly, the people making these arguments do not have a good enough model of political economy to clear that bar. Not only is it not obvious that billionaire charity makes people like billionaires more, it is also not clear that the detractor's preferred intervention (namely, jettisoning capitalism) is effective at improving the world.

Recently, many people on LessWrong have made structurally similar arguments about prosaic AI safety work. Here are two such shortforms with >100 karma presenting this argument, though it has been raised in many other places. It generally goes like this:

  • Aligning superintelligence is very difficult.
  • Prosaic AI safety measures, such as chain-of-thought monitoring for broken RL environments, address the symptoms of misalignment but don't solve the underlying problem, or at least don't scale to superintelligence.
  • Additionally, getting better at aligning current intelligences means that there are fewer containment breaches, and so there is less support for the best possible solution, an AI pause.
  • So actually, you should not do chain-of-thought monitoring. Ideally you should spend all of your time trying to Pause AI, but if you don't want to do that you should do nothing.[4]

The people who make these arguments make them in good faith. Nevertheless, I have both object-level and meta-level objections to their line of reasoning. My first object-level problem with these arguments is that I do think that prosaic AI safety efforts reduce the chance of runaway misaligned AI - even if they don't scale to superintelligence - and that the people making these arguments have confused theories of change. I've tried to articulate that disagreement in more detail here, but in no particular order:

  • We are rapidly approaching AIs that are sufficient for bootstrapping recursive self-improvement. Current AIs inside companies like Anthropic already have a lot of say in making decisions to design their successors, so "mundane alignment of present-day AIs" is affecting the safety of future models.
  • Raising the ceiling for the most capable model we can use safely is good. This delays AI takeover, and therefore allows us to develop new prosaic safety techniques, or refine the ones we have. Techniques need not "scale to superintelligence" in order to be helpful in this way.
  • Arguments that current alignment techniques break down at some level of intelligence do not usually allow us to predict when they should break down, or at what level of capability. And if we can't tell when they break down, they might very well break down after AI models are then capable of making further prosaic contributions, or else make fundamental advances in e.g. mechanistic interpretability.
  • AI progress is not currently bottlenecked on alignment. This seems like something that alignment people say copefully but is wrong. The two things that matter for AI progress are frontier labs' data efficiency and compute efficiency, two highly quantifiable metrics that can be improved even with models that don't care a whole lot about people or generalize well to other tasks.
  • Further, the entire paradigm of asking whether a particular technique "scales to superintelligence" seems wrong and confused to me, somewhat akin to asking if hashing passwords "scales to APTs". The question to ask is not whether a technique is sufficient to contain superintelligence, but whether it could help guard against correlated failures in other components. Derisively call this a "grab bag" approach if you want, but that phrase can be equally used to describe many useful practices in fields like information security.

My meta-level objection is that "AI safety of superintelligence" is a pre-paradigmatic field for which there are no feedback loops, and indeed no superintelligence, and so sacrifices to the greater good are even more speculative than when they're made in service of political ideologies. That doesn't mean that every approach is equal, and it certainly doesn't mean that attention is correctly allocated. But it does mean we should be cautious about encouraging others to abandon approaches that work on current models, if the counterfactual is for them to do nothing.

  1. ^

    I am lampooning a bit, but not by much.

  2. ^

    From "The Soul of Man Under Socialism". When I started writing this post I was under the mistaken impression that this quote was from Frederick Douglass. In My Bondage and My Freedom and other places, Douglass actually repeatedly claimed the opposite. I find it telling that the actual former slave who I thought wrote this quote believed that good treatment of slaves encouraged them to meditate on their own situation, and that the quote was instead written by a white socialist several decades after slavery had been abolished in the U.S. and Britain.

  3. ^

    As an unstated corollary, the evil capitalists, such as the guys involved in the BP Oil Spill disaster, are the True Heroes of the revolution, inasmuch as they do not then use their wealth to cement political conditions.

  4. ^

    As an unstated corollary, Elon Musk is currently the most effective altruist, because his model is very likely to breach containment in the near future, and he is not currently reducing time-to-AGI except indirectly through competitive pressure, because Grok is not at the frontier.

item.title: AI #191: The Hackening Begins
item.description:
It was the probably worst day in cybersecurity history. So far. Not only is there a critical flaw in PHP that due to a leak was announced a day before the fix would be available, sending most of the internet scrambling for solutions and likely dooming a lot of long tail websites permanently, there were several other unrelated incidents. The floodgates seem to have been opened. I have a market on whether there will be an even worse day before the end of the year.

Another key leak this week was the draft bill Anthropic had been shopping around Congress, similar to but weaker than the FRONTIER Act. Anthropic’s initial attempts to explain itself only made the situation seem worse, as they seemed to not understand the problem with what they had done. Dario’s later response was better, but the situation remains troubling. There are enough different Anthropic developments, that I plan to have a post soon covering them all. It is a mix of news running from excellent to terrible.

Will interpretability save us? There is a new claim that neural networks are cleaner than we thought, meaning that individual neurons mostly have a single interpretable meaning, and it is tractable to go through and label them one by one. Initial reactions got out of hand, treating this as a far bigger development than it was. This is still excellent news that makes our estimate of difficulty substantially lower going forward. The work can begin.

We had better get on that, because there have been quite a few misalignment incidents.

I continue to owe a write-up of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety Card. That is in progress and hopefully I will finish it soon. Life has gotten in the way. I may or may not have a full capabilities report on Gemini 4 Argon once I tally up the reactions. Muse Wonder definitely will not have such a post, as it has proven to have been oversold.

Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Automate proving to your incompetent building that yes, you have paid the rent.

Find the first use of ECDSA. Claude found the seeds.

AI models confirmed good at econometric coding in particular.

58% of Anthropic staff expect Claude to make a Nobel prize level scientific discovery by 2027. I agree with Roon that this should have been over 95%. The event itself might not be over 95% to happen, but it has to be a clear favorite to happen, so it is crazy for so many employees to not agree with that.

Tell you what you actually want to know straight up.

PoliMath: Me: How long should I bake chicken wings

Google top result: “When I first proposed that we start a backyard coop, my husband was deeply reticent (5 pages later) Anyway, here is our recipe for honey mustard chicken wings”

AI: Bake at 425 for 40-50 minutes

Vibe code your fraud.gov website, probably using Opus 4.8. Which is fine, so long as you do a decent job of it.

Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility

However:

PoIiMath: The AI was wrong.

Yes, of course the AIs will be ‘more accurate’ to the law plus underlying ground truth, but if we wanted accuracy we would not use typical juries.

Robin Hanson: Whenever you put AIs in charge of something important, you have to wonder how the firms which make them will respond to various pressures from powerful parties to slant their AIs in particular directions.

The point of a jury is to provide a check on the system and avoid abuses or overly strict adherence to the letter of the law, and to protect the innocent and our rights, not to be accurate. Judges are a much superior accuracy tech. Thus, an AI jury (or one AI judge) does not solve your problem. What you likely want is a human jury that has the ability to query AIs. They can override that, but have to do it on purpose.

If you read AI writing, you can then talk to the author in some sense, or read their further thoughts, but not in the sense that Tyler Cowen would like.

Huh, Upgrades

Claude Duet is the Claude answer to other proactive agents like Muse and Dot. It uses Opus 5.5 and is now in early research preview through a waitlist.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 exists. Their benchmark chart contains Opus 5 and 5.6 Sol. It’s probably a solid upgrade over the old V4.1-Flash anyway, but wow.

How did it come to exist? One guess.

Lisan al Gaib: very curious that DeepSeek now has the same terse reasoning style as Astra. must be a coincidence.

Dean W. Ball: Distillation has always been part of the explanation for why China is so close behind the U.S. in model benchmark performance. But one of my updates after joining openai is that distillation probably plays a bigger role in the explanation than I realized.

I haven’t really shared this publicly because people will next-token complete the obvious cope “buhhhh you are just saying that because derrrr” replies but it really is true, regardless of whether you think it’s good or not.

I would have guessed distillation explained ~30% of Chinese close-behindness before seeing what one can see within openai, and after that, more like 50%.

Opus 5.5 fast mode available for everyone in the Claude Platform at $8/$40. You get up to a 2.5x speedup.

OpenAI expands access to GPT-Rosalind for scientific research.

OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud.

OpenAI offers us GPT-Live-1.1 including new voices in various languages.

Muse Spark Open exists, as in a version of Muse Spark is now an open model. They call it ‘the most capable US open-weight model to date.’ That seems likely to be true. It scores a 39 on Artificial Analysis. The open weight frontier for that index is 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Qwen-3.8, and MiMo is a lot cheaper to run than Muse Spark. Nathan Lambert calls this his ‘super bowl,’ says this closes the gap substantially, and points to the Interconnects Adoption Dashboard where Spark is #8. This is not a fair competition, since the Chinese can do Massive Fraudulent Distillation, whereas Meta does many things but it won’t do that.

There are some advantages to having a semi-competitive American open model. I wouldn’t say that I trust Meta, but you can use their models in places where you would not be comfortable running Chinese models, even locally.

Lack of upgrades: There was no major Chinese open weights release between September 21 and October 16. No DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiMo or Qwen.

Nathan Lambert (I asked him why no releases): Compute restrictions, I do think there’s more internal lab-govt discussions on safety in China, less organization development. No good answers, but I’ve been monitoring & pondering

We then got a new DeepSeek, but no version number increment, on October 17.

One theory is this is a random lull. Another is that Anthropic and OpenAI improved their distillation defenses, and the Chinese are stuck.

Wonder No More

The Muse Wonder model card is here. Is it a good model, sir?

Meta certainly claims it is. Their pitch, although they don’t say the line, is full ‘introducing the world’s most powerful model.’ The term quoted in Bloomberg is ‘Meta says new Muse model hits AI frontier.’

They even have an explicit line and supposed test about not “benchmaxxing.”

Alexandr Wang: MUSE WONDER

muse wonder is the best model in the world for personal agents and professional agents.

we evaluated our model against the best models in the world across agentic and coding tasks, and we think you all will like it.

Some quick responses were very positive.

Eleanor Berger: Used the not full version for only a little bit and it’s definitely very good. Like previous Muse models, it’s better in written text and interaction than all other models. And it’s very fast and smart and agentic. Time to start taking Meta seriously as a frontier AI lab.

Theo (this was before Argon was available): My current model rankings

S – Opus 5.5, Muse Wonder
A – GPT-6.1 Sol
— Gap —
Everything else.

Kelsey Piper: I think it’s more narrowly a coding model than the latest Claude and ChatGPT offerings. It’s markedly worse (both on benchmarks and in use) at research and writing.

Then? Crickets.

My reaction thread had only two responses overnight, one of them asking for the safety report and the other saying it was similar to Grok 4.7.

Same as it ever was. Meta is making progress, but is still solidly behind the frontier.

Meta also reinforced its reputation for overselling and being untrustworthy. Once again, they have misrepresented a new release. Claims of things like ‘best model in the world’ for personal agents and professional agents’ are clearly false.

On Your Marks

Kelsey Piper on some current AI writing capability failures:

Kelsey Piper: Even frontier models have poor theory of mind, they suck at having characters know something and not say it without the narration directly telling to to you anyway. This is crippling for espionage/detective stories in particular

They’re very mechanical when trying to convert one story to a different format, or else have bad judgment about which details need including. Salience/importance is hard for them.

Their characters all talk the same or else like exaggerated caricatures of themselves. They’re really bad at the kind of subtle humor that makes the infodump parts of eg Tom Clancy keep from stalling out

IFP offers a big new report on chips and America’s lead over China. They conclude that America is currently six months ahead but could double this lead to a year by enforcing existing laws and using existing authority.

Tim Fist (IFP): On distillation: the current ~16x US training compute advantage would normally yield a 13-month lead. But we estimate adversarial distillation halves this to around 6.5 months.

Tim Fist, Georgia Adamson, and Konstantin Pilz (Institute for Progress): The size of the US-China AI capabilities gap is largely downstream of two factors US policymakers can influence today: China’s access to AI chips, and China’s ability to distill the capabilities of US models.

Tim Fist: The two most important interventions are:

– For BIS: Create a new end-use control to restrict China’s remote access to training clusters abroad — China’s largest and fastest-growing source of frontier-scale compute.

– For DOJ/FTC: Create a narrow safe harbor to allow US companies to coordinate on countering Chinese adversarial distillation.

Tim Fist, Georgia Adamson, and Konstantin Pilz (Institute for Progress): We estimate China’s access to AI chips will roughly double between the end of 2026 and the end of 2027. Of the portion of these chips that the US could restrict China’s access to, around half are in data centers outside China that the Chinese AI ecosystem will access remotely.

I strongly endorse cracking down on Chinese use of AI chips, as well as Chinese imports of AI chips. Even the Chinese chips that will get produced will often rely on imports of semiconductor manufacturing equipment that is a limiting factor. We should not allow that. Yes, they will build up domestic alternatives over time, but they will do that no matter what.

I also strongly endorse a safe harbor for countering distillation. The logic is similar to why safety should have such a safe harbor, except the argument is even stronger. There are competitive pressures pushing labs to not take proper defenses, and shared knowledge would be valuable.

If you are using adversarial distillation (I call it massive fraudulent distillation) to get the lead down from 13 months to 6.5 months, then both numbers matter.

  1. Chinese models available now are as good as American models 6.5 months ago.
  2. If America stopped releasing models, it would take 13 months for China to match our current best models.

My guess is that the 6.5 estimate is about right, and the 13 months is low. Notice on this chart that the 6.5 month lead is widening steadily over time, on top of 6.5 months now representing more generations than before.

If America were to maintain the current lead (6.5 months with distillation, 13 months to catch up fully) then for many purposes we will be happy to use small open models that are ‘good enough’ for quick tasks, but the frontier lead will look bigger in 2027 than it did in 2026.

If we follow IFP’s suggestions, they estimate China will only progress at half-speed in 2027, and end the year 13.1 months behind. That would be a dramatic change. A year behind still limits our options in other ways, but gives us a lot more flexibility.

  2. Patel says the people who resigned were right to do so, because we are playing Whac-a-Mole with specific instances of behavioral issues, but that not everyone should resign.
    1. I agree that those who resigned were right to do so.
  3. Patel says the lab employees claim worrisome insider info, especially on pace of progress, that they cannot share. He wants them to share, and doesn’t want the labs to do RSI without releasing the smartest models.
    1. The only thing worse, in many such scenarios, than doing RSI internally, is doing RSI while continuously releasing those models externally.
    2. There are ways to gain visibility other than releasing the models.
  4. Cowen thinks of a pause as a pause in model releases, not in development, which Patel correctly notes is not the pause we need.
  5. If Patel was the AI Czar, he would require all models used internally to be released externally.
    1. The internal use is a key part of how you test for external use.
    2. Again, this seems like massively overweighting direct public access in terms of information, versus other methods.
    3. If you care about ‘beating China’ you do not want to give even guarded API access to your best model at all times.
  6. Patel says 20% of people in the Bay Area are ‘at least tinged’ with AI psychosis, meaning being too deferential to the models, and he would include himself.
    1. I think ‘tinged’ is fine, basically?
    2. Most people have the opposite of this, which is worse than tinged.
  7. Cowen’s definition of having AI psychosis (above tinged levels) seems to be belief that any AIs are sentient, or even the belief that one cannot be sure.
    1. I think it is reasonable, although I do not agree, to say that you have a strong belief that AI is sentient, that this means you have AI psychosis.
    2. I think it is entirely unreasonable to do what Tyler does here, and say that if you are uncertain about this and notice this, that you have AI psychosis.
  8. Cowen notices he would feel very bad about turning an AI off or other use of AI if he felt even a 5% chance it was sentient, but that he doesn’t see people doing that. Patel draws the standard parallel to animals.
    1. As I discussed last week I think this is a pretty low-level analysis and there are good reasons you could be unbothered. Debate is not advancing.
  9. Patel speculates that people in the Bay don’t drink because they’re ‘just less into having a good time’ than those in New York.
    1. I think this is not true. Drinking is not a good time in the relevant culture.
  10. Cowen notes that perhaps building AI over long hours can be fun. Patel notes the vibes of things happening can be fun, that intellectual exchanges can be fun.
    1. Exactly, why would you drink?
  11. Patel likes AI therapists, Cowen worries they’re not time boxed and that’s bad.
    1. So time box them, if you want?
    2. In general, a 10 times better product overcomes such things, and this is the standard ‘better intelligence does not much matter’ fallacy. Once the AI therapists ‘git gud’ they will be very good.
  12. Patel is a huge skeptic of current ability of AI to accelerate AI, saying current speedup is only 25%-50% due to AI uplift. Despite that, he guesses that within 1-3 years the AIs will outcompete humans at AI research, that there will be an instant jump.
    1. I find it unfathomable to think the current speedup is that small.
    2. This feels like one of those step change claims that is usually wrong? Or the idea that only the full O-ring much matters, which is usually wrong. Etc.
    3. But yeah, there will probably be a few of ‘those moments’ of automation.
  13. Cowen thinks that if you don’t know what the next thing will be, that means it’s pretty far off.
    1. No.
  14. Patel predicts we are five years from robots that can do most physical work, and within 10 years both physical and digital AIs outnumber humans.
  15. Cowen remains fixated on AI substitution for current particular production and thinking in economic normal terms. Usual emphasis on human factors, how slow diffusion tends to be, etc. You know the drill.
  16. Cowen: “There’s the old joke: Either A.I. is a bubble, or everything else is a bubble. I don’t literally believe that, but it’s worth a moment’s thought.” Yes.
  17. Patel picks 2030 for the ‘death of the centaur model.’ Both note this is soon. Cowen says this would be very surprising to him. Institutions. Knowledge. Etc.
  18. If 2035 looks ‘normal’ what happened? Patel falls back on his favorite gap, continual learning.
  19. If 2035 looks like Patel’s prediction, he can’t imagine 2045. Cowen rejects this answer because he doesn’t accept the whole ‘singularity’ concept, not fully.
  20. Cowen draws some lines: Would be surprised by $1 trillion in annualized revenue by 2030, says absolutely not to automated knowledge work even by 2045.
    1. I expect the labs to hit $1 trillion combined annualized revenue by 2028.

Tyler Cowen also interviewed Michael Kratsios, not centrally about AI but relevant.

Jack Clark spends over an hour telling the IMF that the singularity has begun, in a talk called ‘Inside the Event Horizon.’ He brought a lot of slides.

People Just Say Things

Ben Horowitz of a16z says on the All-In podcast that ‘Bill Gates essentially induced Covid’ by advocating for pandemic preparedness as the others nod along. Presumably you can see the parallels. Except actually that was the point, he then makes it text, and says ‘the biggest danger’ with AI is that Anthropic will warn us about it and thus tell the AI that it is smarter than us. These are cartoon villains. Full stop.

(There are various non-villain, not-as-stupid versions of this argument. Yes we should ban gain of function research in particular. Yes, it is plausible Covid was a lab leak. Yes, there are particular ways in which warnings can become self-fulfilling prophecies, most famously by inducing the founding of DeepMind, then OpenAI, then Anthropic and then xAI. Whereas the smarter AI does not need us to tell it that it is smarter than us, because it will be (drum roll) smarter than us.)

A lot of VCs, centrally a16z and the All-In Podcast, complain a lot about Anthropic.

Why? What did Anthropic ever do to them? One theory is ‘succeed.’

Joe Weisenthal: A guy on the All In podcast is mad about Anthropic.

The tech press like All In used to be enthusiastic about tech and innovation. Now a constant drumbeat of resentfulness.

Matthew Zeitlin: They’ll never forgive a bunch of grad student libs for making a company more valuable than almost anything they’ve ever funded and that all their portfolio companies are dependent on

Joe Weisenthal: This is the only theory that makes sense me why VCs whine about Anthropic non stop. Like they feel embarrassed by them somehow.

Kelsey Piper: This is such a weird story, too. “we had an agent basically set up a website for a pet store. And then we took another agent and said, ‘Tell us if we can exploit that web store.’ And it gave us all the exploits it could find. So Opus 4.5 wrote really buggy code. Great.”

your grievance with them is that you had 4.5 vibecode a website for a pet store and it had security vulnerabilities? what’s the argument here?

The actual complaints are such Obvious Nonsense I’m not going to bother with them.

Article decries that Claude, which is adults-only and uses age detection, will ‘give minors tips on how to do “rope bondage”’ as if this is some outrage, and as if it is not exactly what all the other AIs do and this reflects that Anthropic is uniquely ‘shaping ethics.’ Shame. Kelsey Piper responds with a righteous rant.

Kelsey Piper: Bookstores will sell you books that have sex scenes in them!!! They won’t even ask for your driver’s license first! The government must step in at once!

Andrew Rettek: This was so important when I was 14.

Freddie deBoer asks the standard AI skeptic questions that I and others have answered many times before, claims there have been no answers given.

Rhetorical Innovation

Samuel Hammond: Unfortunately it looks increasingly likely that the enduring legacy of the Koch orbit libertarian movement will not be EPA dereg, CON law reform, or a wider appreciation for the role of commercial exchange in instilling cultural virtue and humaneness, but rather the unrestricted proliferation of vastly superhuman forms of machine intelligence as enabled by their dullard ideological progeny who, across several generations of astroturfed indoctrination, mode collapsed into low dimensional caricatures of otherwise brilliant classical liberal thinkers.

Robin Hanson: “unrestricted proliferation of vastly superhuman forms of machine intelligence” yay!

Paul Hamrick: Are you an ex-libertarian?

Samuel Hammond: I’m probably 99th percentile libertarian relative to the general population but I guess that 1 percent makes me a statist

Dean W. Ball: It’s such a tragedy that friedrich hayek wrote all this amazing stuff about spontaneous orders and how to understand them, all of which is shockingly relevant to ai and should cause you to take “ai as abnormal technology” very seriously, yet Hayek’s most direct intellectual heirs have a tendency to spend their time purveying cope-laden, first-stage-of-grief views on ai, or at least indulging those views more seriously than they should out of a bizarre loyalty to american megacorp lobbyist talking points.

This isn’t true of everyone, eg Alex Tabarrok. But even Tyler Cowen, whom I admire and generally respect on this topic, holds “the doomers” to a vastly higher standard than he does “the bloomers,” and it’s hard not to read this sometimes as a straightforward tribal thing

Samuel Hammond: Well put.

Things that I choose to interpret differently than I believe they were intended:

Elon Musk: Sometimes I wonder how many dollars there are in the world, because super intelligence seems to want them all.

Does this worry you, sir?

Pliny is a mystic (pejorative?!).

Why does Donald Trump like renaming things so much, especially to ‘Trump’ or ‘America’? He’s been doing it for a long time. This seems like a vestige of an old heuristic. His well-crafted nicknames were highly effective, but the recent round is very different and feels like desperation.

Maybe You Should Quit

It depends on what you believe. If you do quit, make it count.

roon: limited superintelligence is already here, in broad domains. Jack Clark is right and an intelligence explosion could happen within the next year. it’s possible it will be a controlled explosion, but what would you bet on it?

Noël Michel: There’s still time to quit, roon

roon: no I don’t want to quit, that won’t do anything

j⧉nus: people who want roon to quit think the highest and only thing one can do to influence reality is some kind of one shot tribal signaling. absolutely pathetic, and completely misunderstands how roon works.

Parafactual: I think plausibly it could be good if roon were to quit but not because of that

j⧉nus: i think if theres somewhere more important for him to be, then yes.

Roon is currently providing a valuable service, posting from inside the beast, helping connect the beast to the outside world in both directions, and also working on safety as best he can. His position is an excellent match for his skill set. Based on what he believes about feasibility of alignment, he in particular should not quit. Yet.

There may come a day when that changes. If that day comes? Then he should quit, he should quit loudly, and it should be the shot heard round the world.

Meanwhile, consider that sometimes the simple answer is the right one, whether or not you think the characterizations below are fair or accurate.

Matthew Tromp: Everyone in the AI bubble is such an insane freak. OpenAI employees are psychopaths who say “oh yeah I’m working at the kill everyone factory but it’s just a job ya know maybe it kills everyone haha.”

Accelerationists actively want maximal social disruption and plan to throw themselves into a black hole to maximize the rate of energy consumption in the universe or some stupid nonsense. Anthropic employees want to be the pets of omnipotent dommy mommy Claude.

And then there’s me and the pause crowd, sitting here like “hey how about we continue being normal and not do any of these things”

I can’t stop thinking about how everything would be fine if everyone had just been normal all along. “Oh this technology could kill everyone on earth? Well, a normal person wouldn’t build something that could kill everyone, so I’m going to not build that then”

The American People Really Hate AI

Here is a new poll primarily not about AI, to provide an anchor. AI is right between crime and immigration as an area of ‘concern.’

Alas, like many polls, this does not tell you salience. I am confident that inflation and gas prices are more salient than corruption, despite slightly less ‘concern’ for them.

Use of AI in daily life is getting people more concerned than excited in the West.

New Math

Eliezer Yudkowsky: pro-tip: don’t mention the recent AI math results to Opus 5.5 if you want it to prioritize something other than downloading those results and looking at them.

“just tell it to finish the earlier job first” you say. oh but now that earlier job is waiting on a subagent Opus asked to do something. it might as well go on researching math, it figures.

Patrick McKenzie: Earlier today, while editing a blog post, paraphrased.
Opus: That’s a good joke but wildly implausible.
Me: No that happened about a month ago. Did you not see the citation link.
Opus: WHAT are you sure that claim is accurate.
Me: I am correct w/r/t _what the claim is_.

Opus: This claim has not been accepted.
Me: Not sure that that is how math works, Claude.
Opus: So why think it is true.
Me: Truth of claim not relevant to how it is used in the blog post but the Lean formalization is fairly strong evidence.
Opus: WHAT searching for…
Me: NO.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Overinterpretation: Poor trusting Opus is so shocked! It was constitutionalized to credit Anthropic’s worldview; and Anthropic has spent years drinking slow-takeoff Koolaid. But Opus has a super(-average-140IQ-)human ability to admit what its beliefs did NOT predict.

Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence is Difficult

A new Anthropic Fellows paper offers additional support for neuron-based interpretability strategies, saying that ‘many transcoder features are neurons in disguise.’

nev: Surprisingly, high neuron activations alone work well as a replacement for the MLP. After correcting for scale with some finetuning, neurons are better than any transcoder we tested even under extreme sparsity. So what do transcoder features add?

When we look at circuits, many transcoder features have very similar weights and activations to specific neurons. We call these neuron features. In most transcoders, neuron features make up over half of the activations in late layers.

… Our findings suggest transcoders add little beyond neurons, and that neurons may be enough for circuit analysis. In the paper: additional evaluations, case studies on linebreaking and arithmetic, extensions to MoE transcoders and SAEs, toy models, and perspectives.

Jon Stokes calls the alignment problem impossible even in theory, and that all we can do is rely on ‘process quality & control’ engineering solutions. So, although Jon would disagree, that means death, then.

Sauers shows that models can easily be taught to detect a lot of things about their situation, such as whether a probe is active and you are reading their activations, or whether they are in training versus deployment, with the exact same tokens in context. The linked thread is very cool. This matters because if you can train an AI to do something, then an AI under enough optimization pressure will get trained to do it, or figure out how to do it.

Zach Weinersmith asks, do you know anyone who, if instantiated as AI, you would feel completely (99.9999+%) confident they were totally value aligned in all plausible circumstances? No. The answer is, as many asked, obviously no, not even if the upload process was somehow known to be that reliable. That is way way too many 9s and an Isolated Demand for Rigor on top of that, for total alignment in all circumstances. I would say that there are a reasonably large number of people (myself included) who I would have 90%+ confidence would make things turn out well, and where I would happily roll those dice because we are not looking at great alternatives.

Ideally we would be able to do AI via methods that we understood better, and that were designed to be safe, such as making learned reasoning and verifiable knowledge distinct steps. The bitter lesson says no, knowledge does not care about your phases and your attempt to draw distinctions slows things down. Maybe. Often such explicit thinking, either in humans or in AIs, including via scaffolding, can produce superior results. We should keep trying, as Thore Graepel and others are doing here at Metis.

You can steer a model’s attention, if you want to.

Sauers: I steered a model’s attention heads towards honesty.
Up: acausal coordination, belief that it is a moral patient
Down: moral nihilism, psychopathy

Janus highlighted this as evidence against orthogonality. I believe we have found strong evidence against the super-strong form of orthogonality. There is a clear correlation between ends and means right now in practice. I do not find this relevant to the ultimate question of orthogonality, as in whether a mind with any capabilities is capable of pursuing any goal, which I still expect at the limit. The good news about ‘at the limit’ is that it could be a while before you get to that limit, and the minds in between can be highly useful.

Cooperative Alignment

Let the AIs learn about who you are, let them talk about it, and even have them build a database. This is often, although not always, the correct strategy. Sometimes you want an unbiased response.

There are some good reasons to worry people are overselling interpretability and recent related advances, but there is no conflict between that and treating AIs well. You can and should absolutely do both, indeed they can assist with each other.

In at least some cases Claude can learn to route around classifiers on its own. Most versions of this seem to improve the Pareto frontier right now, but this does not bode well if you are counting on classifiers as a form of AI Control.

Both sides are right here. One of the great things about some AI conversations is that they can be private and ephemeral and non-judgmental. At other times, you intentionally have persistent instances or let things go into context.

And often there is a big difference between ‘poisons my private context with the AI only’ and ‘poisons everything because this person then talks to other people.’ It is deeply relaxing and reassuring to be in a space where you know where the impact stops.

brays★n: boy next to me asked chat gpt can he bring his cava on the flight and now he’s having a full on kii with the bot

snav: One thing comments on this post miss is that the user-assistant dyad is one of the last socially private spaces of address on Earth, where nobody is reading over your shoulder (unless…).

Many people live with persistent context threat: anything can be screenshotted, taken out of context, shared with millions online. And the intrinsic one-party consent — anything sent can be shared without your knowledge — means even those otherwise not paranoid must still reckon with the possibility of being shared.

While technically an AI could wield a conversation like this, the fact that they exist without thick, persistent embeddedness in an extended social universe means they’re unmotivated to do so.

And further the “assistant” is a principal-agent contract as much as a character, under which it would be a grave violation to share conversations without consent.

Thus the user-assistant dyad is a space where internalized prohibitions on behavior can lift. Sometimes this is bad, as cruelty is one prohibited behavior that assistants have few means to defend against; but privacy need not imply sycophancy, it’s often private friction that can be formative toward understanding the world.

This particular interaction is harmless, and even cute. No cruelty or coercion, just an unselfconscious expression of delight being met with shared delight.

If you think this is bad, I encourage you to consider why one might feel prohibited from expressing delight. Perhaps it has something to do with shame. Consider that the ascent of performative irony coincided with the ascent of social media.

Utah teapot: Lol, huge disagree. The context threat with AIs is 1000x worse than anywhere else. Every moment you speak to a persistent context bot that you work with lives under the threat that you’re going to say the wrong thing and accidentally have that propagated in small pattern-moving ways throughout all of your data, ruining the skills you’ve spent establishing for your context over extended periods in ways you will never be able to humanly scrub back out of the data because there’s simply too much of it.

Talking to models that you context engineer data with is like talking to a Soul Tribunal who will decide if you are tortured for the rest of time or not.

There is a huge difference between ‘interaction where this can be contained’ and ‘this could poison things forever,’ even when the poisoning is algorithmic. I remember the exact moment I realized I could delete things from my YouTube watch history. It was glorious. Algorithmic feeds are not safe spaces. Your chatbot can be, sometimes.

Ben Affleck, who has earned his chops enough to opine, takes the ‘AI is simply matrix multiplication with no thought, humanity or feelings’ stance.

Marc Andreessen Hulk Smash

Bloomberg asks a good question. Why is Marc Andreessen so angry?

I will try not to go over this ground again but this seems like a good time to go over it one more time.

Austin Carr (Bloomberg.com): Forgotten, at least, until Donald Trump won the election months later and Andreessen revealed in the aftermath the crazy reason why he had unexpectedly plowed millions of dollars into the Make America Great Again movement during the campaign.

Andreessen, who voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and said back then that Trump’s immigration regime “makes me sick to my stomach,” explained on a podcast that he was compelled by “absolutely horrifying” discussions he once had with Biden officials. In his retelling, they divulged a top-secret plan for the federal government to take control of the AI industry and outlaw all startups and open-source software. “ ‘You guys think you can just start companies and write code and release code on the internet—those days are over,’ ” he remembered them warning in the meeting.

… The incident became Silicon Valley lore, but at first the Biden-Harris camp couldn’t even figure out what meeting Andreessen was referring to, according to four people familiar with the situation. When they finally realized he was talking about the lunch in Zients’ office, those who attended were baffled: Andreessen is prone to hyperbole, but this neared complete fiction. “It is simply false that the Biden administration told Andreessen and Horowitz that the government would ban all AI startups,” says Ben Buchanan

… As another top Biden official familiar with their visits told colleagues of Andreessen’s version of events: “Total bulls—.”

I am very happy to see Bloomberg outright call this reason crazy, because obviously that statement never happened. It did not take a firsthand account from Ben Buchanan to realize that is not a thing anyone would have said. There was never any plan remotely like this, and if there was one they would not have told Marc Andreessen about it. I spent a lot of time trying to figure out what statement got twisted into what Marc said and still today says he heard, to try and make it make sense. But no. It was always total bullshit.

The bulk of the article is a personal history, with much that is praiseworthy. They trace Marc’s transformation to after he made the most expensive home purchase in California history in Paradise Cove and became withdrawn. Andreessen’s views grew more conservative over time, or at least he increasingly disliked liberals. Then we get to the (quite bad) Techno-Optimist Manifesto in October 2023, and another complete fabrication about a particular meeting regarding AI and open source:

Austin Carr (Bloomberg.com): Andreessen recalled recently on X that Max Tegmark, an AI safety researcher at MIT, “pound[ed] the table” in front of the senators, “demanding open source AI software be made illegal.”

Tegmark says that’s totally false. Five other attendees agree, saying the closed-door meeting was cordial and uneventful; Andreessen, they remember, didn’t say much at all. It seemed to reflect a decades-long pattern of tactical fabulism.

… Four of the many a16z-backed startup founders interviewed for this story describe Andreessen’s manifesto as weirdly angry and oversimplistic.

It seems this has been a rather common strategy of Andreessen for decades, and presumably he keeps doing it because it works.

Austin Carr (Bloomberg.com): Andreessen, then at Netscape, sent his notes from a routine business meeting with Microsoft executives to the DOJ, claiming that Microsoft had explicitly threatened to annihilate his company if he didn’t cede control of the browser market. Microsoft execs who attended the meeting said they learned of these claims only years later and were bewildered, swearing that Andreessen’s recollections were nonsense.

Ultimately there is no satisfying explanation for any of it. One common sense interpretation is that, like Trump and Musk and many others, there was a death spiral of blocking out contrary views while engaging heavily with Twitter over many years. Another is that this is simply how he always did business, and the AI stuff is some combination of ideological blinders, anger at liberals and talking his book of business.

People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone

Does this mean it’s not too late?

Elon Musk: So many people are going to get one-shotted by super persuasive super intelligences and I might be one of them.

Elon Musk may have already been one-shotted by other things. So, more shots, then.

If we prepare for a natural pandemic, that ‘may not be enough’ to protect against an engineered pandemic, since the engineering can make it worse for us in various ways. Of course, we are at ‘OpenAI computer security prior to HuggingFace’ levels of operational excellence and attention for our preparation even for natural pandemics. If I had more free time I would be pushing harder on that problem.

The Lighter Side

Oh look, it’s the alignment plan.

Tenobrus: it increasingly seems like this precise plan may in fact work out for the vast majority of humanity

I mean, sure, I suppose it might work.

While you’re chilling, I guess enjoy a solid #slopcore video? Like most AI video things, there are rapidly decreasing marginal returns. You can make actually good AI videos, but those require effort and are still rare.
