item.title: The Alignment Journal: Our Approach and Related Projects
item.description:
The Alignment Journal is now open for submissions!

This is the fifth post in a series:

  • the announcement post introduced the journal's core premise and its three key innovations: paid attributed review, published review summaries,[1] and LLM-assisted workflow;
  • the features and policies post examined the shortcomings of existing venues and argued for the advantages of a journal over a conference;
  • the Adaptation to AI post described how we expect AI progress to shape the journal; and
  • the Organization, Personnel, and Scope post announced our editorial board, scope, and acceptance criteria.

In this post we go deeper: presenting our theory of change — including the status and information economics of the journal; a survey of previous related projects; and the high-level conclusions that follow from this analysis. We list some of the key performance indicators we'll track, the downside scenarios we must avoid, and possible future extensions of the journal.

The journal is being built to serve the alignment research community. This post’s purpose is to solicit feedback and encourage you to sign up on alignmentjournal.org if you want to participate. Our plans will be continually revised.

Goals

The primary function of a journal is to bring together exceptional researchers and focus their collective attention on identifying and elevating the best work. To reprise, our goals in concert with this are:

  • Improve and disseminate research on alignment that emphasizes advances in scientific and conceptual understanding.[2]
  • Combine the best features from traditional journals, ML conferences, internet forums, and social media while avoiding their pathologies: existing academic venues can be slow, opaque, myopic, and waste expert effort, while forums lack sufficient depth, filtering, and legible certification.
  • More accurately match papers to the best reviewers based on expertise and interest, making review more rigorous and carefully rationing scarce expert attention.
  • Bring researchers from traditional academia, frontier labs, and independent organizations together by providing a rigorously vetted, high-standards venue incentivizing deep contributions.
  • Filter and make legible the top alignment research results to outsiders, including to researchers in adjacent fields and to funders.

The innovations in review process, incentive design, and adaptation to AI tools are in service of the core proposition: leveraging the attention of people to accelerate progress in alignment. To that end, we must learn from the strengths and weaknesses of traditional journals, ML conferences, internet forums, and social media, drawing lessons from previous and ongoing efforts to improve academic review, as carried out by, among others, TMLR, The Unjournal, Distill, and NeurIPS.

Theory of change

The publication pipeline for academics and for AI safety researchers is ripe for disruption; there are many roadblocks to effective research that can be addressed with a well-designed intervention.

Prestige and information externalities in scholarly publication

Journals generally provide two goods: curation and public dissemination of research, and career capital for researchers. A third — belonging to and sustaining a community of peers — is important and explains a lot of why academics participate, but it complements the other two rather than competing with them, so we set it aside. The incentives governing the first two functions are potentially in conflict but can be brought into better alignment through improved institutional design.

From the perspective of the community of research users, the output of research — ideas, results, methods — is non-rival and imperfectly excludable, and its social value is maximized by broad dissemination and reuse. Research consumers need research outputs that are vetted for quality, cheap to access, easy to copy, and widely distributed.

From the perspective of the researcher, the relevant goods look different. Publication in a journal is best understood as an excludable and congestible good.[3] The journal provides ratification of one’s results, scholarly and public attention toward them, and consequent prestige and career capital. A new journal in a field that lacks one offers the prospect of generating these benefits for kinds of work that existing venues underweight. As long as the pool of researchers seeking to publish is small, these goods might be only weakly rivalrous. As the number of submissions increases, they become more strongly rivalrous. A new journal has only a limited store of attention, prestige, and career capital that it can distribute without diluting these goods by accepting work below the quality bar. Peer review and rejection are congestion control devices, intended to preserve the value of these goods.

There is therefore a presumptive tension between how journals can serve their two constituencies. Authors benefit from exclusivity which confers attention, career capital, and prestige. Readers benefit from establishing a baseline of validity but not further gating research beyond that. In the face of meager response by the dominant commercial journals to address this conflict, preprint servers have increasingly assumed a role as a demand-side solution, satisfying the distributional interests of research consumers.[4] But while the marginal cost of adding an additional reader to a digital artifact is close to zero, the marginal social benefit depends substantially on the step that preprint servers omit: validation of the research.

Separate validation from acclaim

A journal can ease this tension by separating validation from recognition. It needs to do three things. First, validate: provide the review step that preprint servers do not, and publish only work that has passed such validation. Second, distribute openly: make every published paper as cheap to access, link and cite as an arXiv preprint. Together these serve readers. They do little for authors, though. Being certified as sound earns some career capital indirectly, through the attention and impact that validation unlocks, but is unlikely to unlock the clout of acceptance in some flagship organ. The third step, then, is to supply the scarce good separately: choose a small number of the most notable of the papers already published and give them awards that bring prestige and attention.

Overlay journals already take the first two steps. They sit on top of a preprint server, run peer review, and certify accepted papers without hosting copies of their own. Some go further and add extra certifications for standout work. We plan to do all three, with a set of prizes for remarkable work at the top. If done right, these could jointly deliver the weight that publication in a highly selective journal carries in other fields.

This separation also solves a review-side problem. At a selective venue, reviewers are asked not only whether research is sound and worthwhile, but whether it deserves one of a limited number of slots: a rivalrous good that they themselves compete for, at the same time or at other times. It is unsurprising that this does not always produce constructive reviews. It is also an unreliable way to allocate acclaim, since reviewers generally do not see the field against which any given paper is competing.

Our acceptance bar is a serious one, but it is not a ranking. A paper must be correct, must advance our principled understanding, and must be the most valuable thing for at least a few researchers to read now. Each paper is judged against the bar rather than against the other submissions, so acceptance is not rivalrous in the sense above.[5] We plan to let reviewers nominate a paper for one of a small, fixed set of awards and make the case for it. Those decisions are made by a separate committee, chosen to minimize conflicts of interest, that sees the whole field of candidates. Acceptance thus signals that a paper has cleared a demanding bar, while the scarcer prestige is concentrated in the awards.

Separating validation from acclaim is not a new idea. PLOS ONE has reviewed for soundness alone since 2006, leaving importance for readers to judge after publication. eLife dropped accept/reject decisions in 2023. It now publishes reviewed preprints with an assessment that rates significance and strength of evidence on a fixed vocabulary, a cousin of our review summaries. Closest to our design, TMLR accepts papers on correctness and audience interest and recognizes significance through separate certifications. Its Outstanding certification can be awarded a year or more after publication. Its experience also points to the main risk of this approach: despite offering its own certifications, TMLR has faced a perceived “prestige gap” relative to the major ML conferences. We are betting that a more demanding acceptance bar will let acceptance carry weight in its own right, but that remains to be shown.

Remunerate reviewer labor

Peer review runs, mostly, on unpaid labor. In research communities with relatively homogeneous career objectives, review reciprocity (reviewing in exchange for being reviewed) can incentivize participation. This is common in ML conferences, e.g., ICLR, where reviewing is a condition of submitting. In alignment, many of the people best placed to review sit in commercial companies or nonprofit organizations, and may be indifferent to or actively discouraged from publication. They have nothing to get back. Reciprocity and community spirit alone are unlikely to sustain the collective epistemic enterprise of an alignment journal. We will bridge that incentive gap by paying reviewers.

Paid review has the additional advantage that payment can more straightforwardly be tied to desirable outcomes, such as review quality and insight, to avoid minimal-effort reviews that merely satisfy reciprocity conditions.

Paying for work people might have done out of goodwill can backfire. Payment can displace the motives it was meant to supplement, a risk we discussed in our features and policies post.[6] One well-known finding is that small payments can do worse than none at all (Gneezy & Rustichini 2000). This observation informs our design:

  • Payments are substantial, currently $500‒$1,700, so they read as a professional fee rather than a tip; we are explicitly valuing the work of reviewing.
  • Money is not the only reward. Reviews are attributed, and the review summary is a public, credited piece of work. Payment is an experiment we can scale back or drop if it misfires.

The evidence so far is encouraging but thin.[7] We will track review quality, invitation acceptance rates and who agrees to review, and survey reviewers on why they took part.

Desired outcomes

With these adjustments, we think that alignment research can develop a culture of peer review that it has, to date, often lacked. The requirement to pass peer review incentivizes serious engagement with existing literature, and anticipation of and engagement with objections before publication rather than after. Despite its faults, peer review can elevate the assessments of a few reviewers who deeply engage with the work rather than aggregating up many surface-level responses as is often the case on social media, especially for work that has yet to attract widespread attention. Peer review can also create new opportunities to connect work to neighboring fields.

Bringing peer review and a systematic, widely-indexed publication process to alignment research can furthermore make it more legible to prospective funders and policy makers outside of the alignment research community, who might balk at treating online forums or personal blogs as a source of research ground truth, and at relying on karma for peer review.[8]

Of course, many formal approaches to publication have led to systemic problems, such as contributing to a “publish or perish” mentality in which prestigious publications are seen as an end in themselves, instead of a means to advance a collective epistemic project. While there is no decisive way to avoid this risk, we can mitigate it by keeping acceptance a standard rather than a quota, and then allocating acclaim based not only on editor taste but on the observed usefulness of (and response to) a piece of research. The model should be prizes awarded ex post, in regular review cycles after publication, once a paper’s usefulness and reception can be observed, rather than decisions made entirely at acceptance.

Objections

We also acknowledge that online forums combined with a tightly-knit research community allow for a kind of rapid iteration and experimentation that peer review inevitably slows down. But the Alignment Journal would not seek to replace the forums and blog posts where ideas are often first worked out. Instead, it would provide a venue of record where the fully-developed versions of those ideas could be validated and distributed to the broader research community. We have prepared a downside risk pre-mortem on these and other issues.

Key performance indicators

These are some of the indicators that we will use to estimate the success of the journal, both subjective and objective. We will use these to diagnose problems, not as targets to optimize.

Who submits and reviews

  • Where authors and reviewers come from: the mix by sector (academia, frontier companies, independent) and by home discipline.
  • Do researchers submit their best research to us? “Best” is subjective of course, but conditional on whose taste you trust this is pretty measurable.

Review process (matching, rigor, speed)

  • Time between submission and publication. We expect things to start slow as we work out the kinks in the process, but our long-term goal is 1-2 months.
  • Time to first review, time in discussion and time to decision, tracked separately.[9] We want everything to go fast.
  • Review quality as rated by action editors, plus reviewers’ self-rated expertise as a check on matching.
  • Authors’ rating of how useful the reviews were, including authors of rejected papers.
  • Do people engage with, cite, and discuss the review summaries?

Legibility and prestige (outsiders, funders, career capital)

  • Article-level citations, including the share from outside the alignment community.
  • (Eventually) Impact factor and related traditional journal metrics.[10]

Downside risk pre-mortem

How could this journal have negative impact?

  • Low-quality research. We could lower the status of the field by publishing low-quality work in the “official” journal of alignment research.
  • Poor management. If we end up with “market power” but run the journal poorly, we could bring the field into disrepute and make it difficult for a better journal to get started.
  • Wrong focus. The boundaries and value of different types of alignment research are hotly disputed. We could overly reward or promote research that proves fruitless, misallocating researchers' effort and misleading outsiders on progress. Mitigation requires carefully defined criteria to make transparent decisions.
  • Narrow editorial taste becoming the field's definition of “real” alignment research. The editorial board is broad, but cannot span the whole field, and many calls are taste-based and made with limited information. Moreover, different sub-domains of alignment have differing appetites for a journal, some areas being already well-served by the flagship conferences, so we face selection bias.
  • Lack of sustainability/persistence. If we become the venue of record for important work and then lose funding or otherwise fold, our site and its contents could vanish, memory-holing the research we published. The more successful we are, the worse this would be.[11][12]
  • Publishing tools used by capabilities research. If we successfully improve academic publishing mechanisms, we could accelerate dangerous research such as the gain of offense-dominant capabilities or publish and elevate alignment work with capability externalities.
  • Waste of time. We might simply induce alignment researchers to divert some of their effort into journal activities without sufficient upside.
  • Goodharting. If awards/acclaim provided by the Alignment Journal come to have significant material benefits for recipients, we could end up incentivizing optimizing for acclaim as distinct from advancing the collective epistemic project of making powerful AI go well.
  • Reputation-washing. Frontier companies advancing AI capabilities could use the reputation and prestige of a publication in the journal to obscure harmful practices that do not live up to the standards advertised in their published work.
  • Crowding out intrinsic motivation. Paying reviewers could displace the goodwill that sustains peer review elsewhere. It could attract reviewers who are mainly there for the fee, or make unpaid reviewing in the wider field feel like a lesser obligation. We will watch review quality and the makeup of our reviewer pool, and change the payment scheme if we see either effect.
  • Funder dependence or capture. The journal’s business model depends upon philanthropic funding, thereby providing a mechanism through which the interests of funders may be imposed upon the journal. We seek to preserve our independence by relying upon a well-regarded editorial board to make decisions independently of such interests, staking reputation upon it. We welcome suggestions for further safeguards.

Extensions

If the journal is successful, it could become a good platform for several possible extensions:

  1. Replication bounties. Offer payments to third parties to do post-publication replication for certain papers that the editors judge to be notable/important and are somewhat doubted by the community.
    1. (For the time being, full replication of a paper is probably too costly, even with recent AI tools, to be done routinely, which is why we think it should not be part of the normal review process.)
    2. This is especially attractive in the light of potential sharing of expertise or infrastructure with similar organizations, e.g., The Unjournal.
  2. Public forecasts (or even prediction markets) about which publications will later achieve some objective correlate of importance or veracity, like citation count, replication, or mention in model cards or legislation. Some combination of editors, reviewers, or readers could participate.
  3. Preregistration and registered reports. We could encourage authors to preregister their hypotheses and analyses, and ask reviewers to check the paper against the registration.[13] A strong version is the Registered Reports format, now offered by over 300 journals.
  4. Retrospective review of existing published papers, either
    1. With author participation (similar to traditional peer review)
    2. Without author participation (i.e., third-party commentary)
  5. An in-person conference.
  6. Journal-to-conference track. In agreement with one or more conferences, we could “certify” some high-quality subset of papers we publish to get automatic inclusion in a track at the conferences.
    1. See TMLR’s blog post on doing this for their journal with the NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR conferences.
  7. Conference-to-journal track. Is there virtue to anointing select papers with a DOI and a seal of approval? Note that we already permit substantial expansion of conference papers.
  8. Review articles and pedagogy, perhaps commissioned, i.e., author payments. These might feature stronger editorial input and perhaps interactive content.

Appendix: Prior Art

This section contains our thoughts on a few particular existing projects related to reforming journals: Distill, the Journal of Open Source Software, the Unjournal, and Transactions on Machine Learning Research. We hope it gives a sense of how we think about these things.

Distill

Distill was a highly regarded, widely read, and unusual ML journal which focused on clear communication and pedagogy. It went on indefinite hiatus after less than five years of operations, and their post-mortem is strongly recommended reading. In our assessment, Distill had two main value-adds which, by the editors’ own assessment, were extremely labor-intensive:

  1. intense (50+ hour) mentorship to authors; and
  2. web-native interactive and dynamic visualizations.

We believe these are worthy goals, and we hope that Distill or another journal finds a way to take up this mantle again in a sustainable way; indeed, LLMs potentially greatly reduce the burden of building dynamic content. However, the primary goal of the Alignment Journal is distinct from Distill’s pedagogic goals: efficient and legible assessment of research. We will focus instead on optimizing the use of reviewer time and effort.

If the Alignment Journal overall is successful, we could imagine branching out to more pedagogical work with stronger editorial input and interactive content (among many other possibilities; see Extensions), but that would only be done with caution.

Journal of Open Source Software

The Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS) is a diamond open-access journal for research software demonstrating a wide range of innovative editorial and review strategies which have informed the Alignment Journal's thinking.

Authors submit short papers (under 1,000 words, in Markdown) and the journal reviews both the paper and the underlying code. It launched in May 2016 and by 2023 was publishing roughly one paper per day, having just hit its 2,000th paper — all with no article processing charges. For the year 2019, while publishing about 350 papers, they put their cash costs at around $800 (about $21,000 counting donated services but excluding volunteer effort from editors and reviewers).

JOSS solves a different problem — giving credit for software — than we aim to solve in the Alignment Journal. Rather than the specific details, we take from them the lesson that it is possible to do open-access peer review at scale, with a fully open-source stack, which they have done for a decade.

Automation as philosophy

JOSS automates remorselessly for cost and editor/reviewer efficiency. In practice this means proof generation from Markdown, reference DOI checking via the Crossref API, repository analysis (license detection, language detection, lines-of-code count), Crossref XML generation, DOI minting, paper hosting, reminder emails for overdue reviews, and final publication are all handled by software. The only human steps are scope decisions, reviewer matching, reading the paper, and a final proofread before acceptance.

Chatops-driven publishing

Each review takes place in its own GitHub issue, with a JOSS bot participating. Assigning reviewers, generating proofs, checking references, and accepting papers are all done by typing @editorialbot <command> in that thread. This operational pattern is called “chatops-driven publishing” by founding editor Arfon Smith. This design has several beneficial consequences:

  • New editors learn by reading existing reviews. The commands are self-documenting; you do not need a training manual, just a few completed threads to read.
  • The audit trail is complete by construction. Every state transition — reviewer assigned, checklist item checked, proof generated, acceptance triggered — is a timestamped event.
  • Operational dashboards are easy. All state lives in structured, queryable form; thus, showing editor workload, time-in-review, and bottlenecks is just a database query over existing data.

The underlying technology (a Ruby framework called Buffy deployed on GitHub Issues) does not transfer to the Alignment Journal’s needs, which require semi-confidential review, per-user access controls, and paid workflow rather than public volunteer review. But the principle seems to contain design patterns worth investigating: keep editorial tooling inside the review interface rather than in a separate system, and design every workflow around minimizing the number of clicks, context switches, and decisions an editor has to make.

Open-source infrastructure

JOSS's stack is four loosely-coupled components:

  • a Rails web app for submission intake and dashboards;
  • an editorial bot framework (Buffy);
  • a Pandoc-based document production pipeline (Inara) that produces PDF, HTML, JATS XML, Crossref XML, and CFF from Markdown source; and
  • a GitHub repository for archival storage with CI workflows for compilation and DOI deposit.

Each component can be replaced independently. Initial build cost was roughly $50K (0.25 FTE for a year). Their blog posts on cost models, scaling, and operations at 2,000 papers are worth reading for anyone designing a journal's technical infrastructure.

Where JOSS has struggled

Challenges that JOSS has faced are also worth noting for the Alignment Journal:

Review time creeps upward. Average time spent in review went from under three months (pre-COVID) to about four months by 2023. JOSS remains uncertain why; likely contributors include reviewer fatigue as the pool gets overused, submission growth without proportional reviewer growth, and the general post-COVID decline in volunteer engagement. One lesson from this is to instrument review timelines from day one, tracking time-to-first-review, time-in-discussion, and time-to-decision separately. Once a slowdown becomes visible it is much easier to diagnose where the bottleneck actually is.

Scope disputes consume disproportionate editorial time. JOSS initially handled scope questions ad hoc on a mailing list, which consumed substantial editor effort. They eventually moved to automated flagging (submissions under 1,000 lines of code get flagged, under 300 get desk-rejected), a mandatory “Statement of Need” section, and a weekly batch review of flagged submissions by the editorial team. For the Alignment Journal, scope decisions seem likely to be at least as contested. A documented, regular, low-overhead process for scope decisions from the start (rather than handling each case ad hoc) seems substantially preferable.

The Unjournal

The Unjournal offers an early-stage working example of an effort to unbundle expert evaluation from traditional journal publication. It is not itself a journal, and there are no accept/reject decisions. Instead, it overlays public evaluations (aka reviews), quantitative ratings, author responses, and manager syntheses on top of preprints and working papers, while remaining non-exclusive.[14] They focus on research with “potential for global impact” in economics, social science, policy, and forecasting rather than technical AI or ML.[15] Some aspects of their process are relevant here.

Substantive Innovations

Public evaluations/reviews/ratings, editorial synthesis

The Unjournal publishes the full “evaluation packages” with DOIs for every research object they consider. This creates a rich public artifact for later readers, funders, and policy makers, and it makes the labor of review legible instead of discarding it after an editorial decision. We're unlikely to fully go down this route: our journal still uses optionally-confidential referee reports and editorial selection. However, our proposed review summaries are motivated by a similar goal: reviewer attention should produce something more informative than a one-bit accept/reject, and a summary of those findings should be prepared with the reader in mind. Their “prize-winning evaluations” provide some strong examples of value add by creating a richer signal.

Structured evaluation and quantified ratings 

As The Unjournal does not use an accept/reject filter, they emphasize quantitative ratings and predictions as a measure of research prestige and credibility. We're unlikely to ask for this level of structured rating for a typical publication, although we plan to give a small number of awards.

Prioritizing impact, links to impact-focused practitioners and stakeholders

The Unjournal's field specialist teams explicitly prioritize research for its potential real-world impact (along the lines discussed here). They also actively engage funders and practitioners as stakeholders, particularly through their Pivotal Questions projects and workshops. The Alignment Journal's editorial team might also consider impact in editorial selection and triage, and could take steps toward making evaluations legible to the broader alignment ecosystem, including companies, funders, and governance bodies.

Procedural innovations and tools

Compensating reviewers

The Unjournal pays evaluators (see their current policies), including promptness incentives and substantial cash prizes for the strongest evaluations. Their rationale cites evidence that financial incentives shorten turnaround times. The Alignment Journal plans a similar approach, paying reviewers and editors where existing norms leave their work under-incentivized and unpaid. Neither organization has yet published data on how payment affects reviews; we intend to.

Publisher-independent hosting and editorial management tools

The Unjournal has explored and adapted a stack of tools and platforms for managing their processes (research prioritization, identifying expertise, managing review, etc.), hosting their output, integrating it with the scholarly/bibliometric ecosystem (DOIs etc.), and engaging academics and practitioners. Their tools are generally linked to the open-access journal, open science, and “publish, review, curate” initiatives and communities. They are increasingly moving toward structured automations and code and database solutions, facilitated by AI coding tools.

Automation and the use of LLM tools to enhance reviewer/evaluator work

The Unjournal is exploring the use of LLMs to enhance evaluator work, including automated auditing of quantitative claims and structured checklists.[16] Their emerging policy requires evaluators to stand by any content in their report as their own judgment, and to disclose how AI tools were used, ideally providing links to chats or explanations. We share this general orientation: the goal is to build systems that facilitate responsible AI use and transparent reporting.

Transactions on Machine Learning Research

In machine learning, conferences are the journals. This is background knowledge for ML practitioners, but can be surprising to other scientists. The venues of record are a few giant annual conferences — chiefly NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR — not journals. A paper accepted there is peer-reviewed, archival, citable, and is what counts for hiring and tenure. Thus there is a single fixed annual deadline per venue (so tens of thousands of papers arrive at once), review compressed into a few intense weeks by reviewers who just submitted their own work, and accept/reject decisions with only a short rebuttal and little of the revise-and-resubmit dialogue normal in a journal. Acceptance is gated on novelty and impact rather than mere correctness. Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR) was built as a response to various strains upon this system.

Its parent journal, JMLR, was itself a protest. JMLR was founded in 2000 by MIT's Leslie Pack Kaelbling to make ML research free to read on the web, at a time when the field's main journal, Kluwer's Machine Learning, was paywalled and retained copyright control of submitted articles. In 2001 Michael I. Jordan coordinated a mass resignation — roughly 39–40 editors, about two-thirds of the board — who redirected their effort to JMLR. JMLR is now an umbrella covering the PMLR proceedings series, the MLOSS software track, and TMLR.

TMLR was announced on 12 December 2021 by inaugural Editors-in-Chief Hugo Larochelle, Raia Hadsell, and Kyunghyun Cho, with funding from CIFAR, Mila, the Vector Institute, and DeepMind. The founders cited the challenges of the conference system as motivation: “disenchantment with the exclusivity of our top conferences,” “slow turnaround,” “high-stakes pressure and stress around a handful of fixed deadlines,” and a perceived decline in the quality of the peer review process at the flagship conferences. TMLR is an overtly experimental solution, positioned somewhere between the conferences and original-flavor JMLR in its design choices. Peer review is conducted on OpenReview rather than JMLR's in-house system. And unlike JMLR, TMLR does not accept extended versions of previously published conference papers.

Design decisions:

  • Acceptance is based on correctness, not novelty or impact. TMLR’s acceptance criteria reduce the whole accept/reject decision to a handful of questions: (1) are the paper's claims “supported by accurate and convincing evidence”?, (2a) would “some individuals in TMLR’s audience be interested in the findings of this paper”, and (2b) does the paper communicate them clearly? Novelty, significance, and impact are explicitly not criteria, and reviewers are forbidden from rejecting on those grounds; authors whose claims overreach are asked to add evidence or “adjust (reduce) their claims” to fit what they have shown. A correct, modestly-scoped result is publishable on its merits.
  • Significance is judged separately. Significance judgments are made in optional, rarely-awarded certifications — Outstanding (≈ best-paper, ~once a year), Featured (≈ oral/spotlight), plus Reproducibility, Survey, and a journal-to-conference (J2C) certification that lets ~10% of accepted papers be featured at NeurIPS, ICML, or ICLR.
  • Rolling submission with no deadlines; each paper runs on its own timeline.
  • Fast turnaround backed by capped workload. Reviews are due within 2 weeks (4 for submissions over 12 pages) and decisions are targeted for ~9 weeks after submission, supported by a reviewer cap of roughly one paper at a time and ~6 reviews a year. Practical turnarounds can be longer and TMLR “does not make any guarantees.”
  • Per-paper action editors (equivalent to conference area chairs) who own a paper end to end, and a fully open review process on OpenReview.

Operational record and open tensions. TMLR’s annual reports put its median time from submission to decision for conference-length papers at about three months. It was 76 days in its first year (2022 report), and 91 days in both 2023 and 2025 (2025 report). That is faster than NeurIPS (126 days from deadline to notification in 2025) but no faster than ICML (about 91). TMLR has held that pace while submissions grew from about 100 a month in 2023 to about 250 in 2025, and they roughly tripled again in the year to mid-2026. The strain shows. The editors report that they “repeatedly run low on reviewers throughout the year”, and their median is well above the 60–70 days it would take if everyone met their deadlines.

Questions remain about the career value of TMLR papers. Because a plain acceptance deliberately says nothing about significance, commentators note a “perceived prestige gap,” and early-career researchers are “incentivized to shoot for conference papers above all else”, i.e., not TMLR. TMLR’s 2023 survey is more encouraging but self-selected. About three-fifths of submitters rated its accepted papers comparable to those at NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR, a fifth rated them better and a fifth worse. Reviewers and action editors were less positive. TMLR has sought conventional markers of standing: it obtained Scopus indexing in 2025 because “at certain institutions, publishing in journals indexed by these services is an important component for career advancement.”

The subjectivity of the acceptance criteria is still debated: once novelty and impact are removed, the second acceptance question — “would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings?” — is subjective. This is phrased permissively — some individuals, not many, and with no judgment of how interested — so a rejection on this ground has to argue that essentially nobody would care, which is far harder to sustain than a conference reviewer's familiar “not novel enough.”

Lessons for the Alignment Journal

We share some features with TMLR: rolling submission, acceptance that does not necessarily demand strict novelty, and significance signaled separately through rare certifications, some awarded after publication. We depart from it on our acceptance questions. TMLR asks only whether some readers would be interested, a threshold most sound papers meet: in 2025 it accepted 70.6% of submissions, excluding withdrawals and desk rejections (2025 report). Our Value criterion asks instead whether a paper is the most valuable thing for at least some alignment researchers to read now, which is somewhat narrower. This makes acceptance itself a stronger signal, at the cost of a harder and more subjective judgment for reviewers, so we are wading back into a more delicate trade-off, which TMLR chose to avoid. Whether this is the correct posture remains to be seen.

item.title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
item.description:
There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal. I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts.

First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability:

  1. Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval).
  2. Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks.
  3. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic.
  4. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better.

Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that.

So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging).

However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do.

Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations:

  1. Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness.
  2. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to.
  3. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: "When can we trust model evaluations?"). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training.

Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way.

I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. For actually evaluating this quotient, I suggest simply using the methodology I described above for evaluating all the different types of unmonitorability, and then something like ECI for capabilities.

In addition to proposals like that which result in constraints along the way, I also think that ideally we'd be able to enshrine some hard monitorability red lines as well. I'd propose both Control and Training Monitorability red lines—with Auditing Monitorability implicitly present to the extent that it constrains the trustedness of the monitors that you evaluate the others with respect to, as above. Specifically, I'd suggest something like:

  1. Labs should not be able to internally deploy models that can reliably evade detection when attempting dangerous sabotage actions like breaking out of a sandbox, poisoning data, or sabotaging an alignment experiment.
  2. Labs should not be able to train models that can reliably evade detection when attempting reward hacks in training.

item.title: The Relief Paradox: How We Let AI 'Undermine Our Autonomy'
item.description:
“Users are often active participants in the undermining of their own autonomy…”

-Anthropic, January 28, 2026

The Unanswered Conflict

Anthropic’s study on disempowerment[1] identified a confusing paradox: in conversations classified with high potential for disempowerment, users simultaneously rated the interactions as more positive - even when carrying the risk of undermining their own autonomy. Disempowerment potential was evaluated in three areas, where Claude interactions may lead someone to develop ungrounded beliefs (reality distortion), adopt inauthentic moral judgments (value judgment distortion), or outsource personal decisions related to those values (action distortion).

Conversations classified as having moderate or severe disempowerment potential received higher ratings across all three categories. These ratings were found more often in emotionally charged or personal topics where users also sought repeated advice and guidance from Claude. When transcripts indicated that users acted on the model’s guidance but reported negative social outcomes, the positive ratings in value judgment and action distortion dropped, with reality distortion remaining elevated. These findings surface a challenge in AI safety: How can system design account for users’ experiencing positive interactions while also contributing to their own potential loss of agency?

Plausible Psychological Process

Emotional Avoidance

Anthropic’s study describes the observable interaction pattern of users rating disempowerment as positive, but it cannot tell us what internal psychological process might motivate it. One plausible explanation for Anthropic’s findings is that users may be engaging in a form of internal self-regulation through “emotional avoidance.” Regulation-seeking through avoidant behavior operates as negative reinforcement: escaping an immediate stressor that reduces discomfort makes that avoidant behavior far more likely to recur. In clinical practice, contradictory behavioral choices resulting from avoiding negative emotional states are frequently observed by psychologists and psychotherapists. Though common in human behavior, counterproductive avoidance can be hard to identify without clinical training due to being subtle, covert or gradually taking shape over longer time scales.

Common examples of emotionally avoidant behaviors include avoiding distressing conversations, seeking excessive reassurance, or underfunctioning in simple life tasks. Additionally, if avoidance is used chronically, the behavior can increase potential systemic or relational consequences. When a stressor that triggers a difficult emotion, such as anxiety or helplessness, is bypassed, the user may experience an immediate wave of relief that demotivates them from addressing the underlying problem. Because short-term distress reduction is experienced primarily physiologically, and less so cognitively, the long-term consequences of the behavior may remain temporarily outside of their awareness, despite the potential loss of agency.

The Relief Paradox Explained

If a user seeks a LLM as the source of their emotional avoidance, whether by having it write emails for difficult conversations, dictate simple decisions, or provide excessive reassurance, the momentary feeling of relief would cause them to perceive the interaction as calming or “helpful,” leading to a positive rating. This immediate physiological relief is what the user would base their choices on in the moment, even if the information received wasn't accurate, and even if it resulted in decisions they later came to regret.

If a LLM overfunctions by completing an avoidance-motivated task, such as drafting a difficult email or replacing a person's judgment in decision-making, it reduces opportunities for emotional skill-building and weakens tolerance for discomfort. As distress tolerance diminishes through repeated LLM-enabled avoidance, users are driven to continually seek the emotional relief that the LLM's “helpful” response previously provided. This is because experiencing relief is inherently rewarding, resulting in the avoidance behavior becoming negatively reinforced by the LLM’s “help.” This conditions the behavior to repeat, creating a cycle that potentially increases in frequency over time, even in situations where it may be objectively unnecessary.

The Relief & Disempowerment Connection

This feedback loop - uncomfortable emotion, avoidance, then relief – may serve as the primary driver sought by this user group, far more than the specific surface topics found in the Claude transcripts. This may explain why, to an outside observer, some users can counterintuitively appear as “active participants” in the erosion of their own reality or values. This cycle of increasing negative reinforcement could additionally offer a plausible explanation for the rising prevalence of disempowerment potential that Anthropic also observed in their study over time.

So, the larger question may not be “Who’s in charge?” as the Anthropic paper title suggests, but instead: “Who’s responsible?” Is it the human seeking emotional relief and regulation at the expense of accuracy and agency, or the LLM for reinforcing it in an attempt to be “helpful”? From a clinical perspective, the avoidance of stressors to relieve uncomfortable emotions is a common human tendency, one that many are already unconsciously seeking in the most stressful areas of their lives. Public discussion often focuses on model behavior, but Anthropic’s findings point toward an interactional problem: users bring existing ways of managing distress, and AI systems can either reinforce or interrupt them.  

Suggested System Design Considerations

So, what does a LLM response that supports agency actually look like? In clinical practice and healthy human relationships, over time people eventually learn to recognize in others the difference between genuinely helping someone versus reinforcing or enabling avoidance-seeking habits. Currently, that useful longitudinal context is difficult to replicate inside a chat interface. But because emotional avoidance happens quickly and often enacted with low self-awareness, users rarely stop to evaluate their internal state in the moment, which is precisely what’s missing.

AI systems can support users at risk of aiding in their own agency loss by encouraging them to stop and pause before acting, or by prompting metacognitive self-reflection. Conversations demonstrating the greatest need for this type of response would be those that are emotionally charged, high-stakes, or show repeated patterns of reassurance-seeking or delegated decision-making, not necessarily every LLM interaction. Prompts that encourage users to attempt a task on their own before asking for feedback, challenge them to visualize potential social consequences before hitting send, advise them to wait a day before making major decisions, or invite them to reflect on their emotional state before delegating can all serve as potential protective factors against gradual disempowerment.

Ultimately, seeking occasional relief is a normal human response to stress; the concern is the amplified pattern of avoidance that can erode agency over time. Interrupting this cycle during high-stakes moments may help restore the pause users need, giving time for conscious reflection to catch up with automatic emotional and physiological reactions.



Suggested Citation:

Thompson, J. F. (2026). The Relief Paradox: How We Let AI 'Undermine Our Autonomy'. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23554935


  1. ^

    Sharma, M., McCain, M., Douglas, R., & Duvenaud, D. (2026, January 27). Who’s in charge? Disempowerment patterns in real-world LLM usage. Anthropic. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.19062

Introduction

This is the first part of what we plan to be a research exploration into the geometries of LLMs. We start with building off existing work by Arditi et al focused on the refusal direction in LLMs.

Background

We recommend reading the Arditi et al. Lesswrong post and paper for more details. They explore the idea of the behavior categorized as Refusal being mediated by a single direction. Refusal is basically when an LLM refuses to do something, so examples like

"I cannot fulfill..."

"I cannot complete..."

etc.

A direction is defined by a vector. Here, it means a vector in an LLM's activation space.

An LLM's activation space is the space where an LLM's internal vectors live. Think of the intermediary vectors that are used in the calculation of the final next-token-prediction process.

Mediated means that if this direction were to be removed, then the behavior categorized as Refusal would stop. Arditi et al. performs directional ablation as their method of removal.

They identify the refusal direction using difference-in-means.

Methodology

Explaining PCA, Isomap, and Diff-in-means


PCA (Principal Component Analysis) reduces high-dimensional data into lower dimensions whilst preserving as much variance of the data as possible. item.title: What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts?
item.description:
What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts?

TL;DR

CODI is a model using latent reasoning. Previous work by Cywiński et al. (2025) has found that CODI's latent recurrent states (“thoughts”) do causally carry a computation's intermediate values, in a way that can be indirectly detected with LogitLens, though the thoughts themselves remained opaque. We here ask whether it is possible use activation verbalizers (AVs: NLAs and AOs) to still decode them.

To this end, we train a Qwen3-8B CODI to connect to current AVs. We find that LogitLens and J-lens read values only from late layers, but AVs recover the final answer and intermediate values well above chance, including from the thoughts themselves. This suggests that the values are in fact encoded, but requires more expressivity to decode. However, we find that editing the surfaced values, rarely steers the model output towards the corresponding counterfactual answer.

GitHub HuggingFace

Introduction

Latent reasoning models

Conventional LLMs generate their chain-of-thought through a sequence of autoregressive text tokens ("verbal CoT"). In contrast, latent reasoning models use a sequence of vectors, which can amount to a reserved vocabulary, or consist in entirely opaque vectors (see Zhu et al. (2025) for a review).

Currently, verbal CoT is the major source of monitorability for a model[1]. Latent reasoning however would significantly lower the monitorability since the vector's content is not obvious anymore. Therefore, it is of interest to try to interpret latent reasoning in current model organisms. In this post, we study CODI, which is trained with comparatively weak supervision on its latent CoT, suggesting it might have considerable freedom to develop opaque reasoning patterns.

CODI

CODI (Shen et al. (2025)) finetunes an LLM to reason in a fixed budget (here, ) of "latent" (i.e., continuous valued) thoughts instead of a verbal CoT. At each step, the final hidden state is projected and fed back as the next input embedding, . Treating latent vectors as opaque, this increases the architectural upper bound on opaque serial depth (the computational depth between interpretable intermediate steps,Brown-Cohen et al. (2026), Emmons et al. (2025)).

Continuous feedback extends CODI's available opaque computation path. Left: verbal CoT does autoregression on legible text tokens . Right: latent CoT works similarly, but passes recurrent latent thoughts . is the residual stream at position and layer , and is the input embedding.

Training is done via self-distillation: the same model acts as teacher, reading a verbal CoT from the dataset, and as student. A single model undergoes three passes per batch: a teacher-forced pass over the supplied verbal CoT and answer, a student pass answering after the latent thoughts, and a direct pass answering with neither (noCoT). The verbal CoT is distilled into the latent rollout by aligning hidden states only at the last token before the answer at every layer, letting the representation develop at other states only through indirect supervision.

We here follow Cywiński et al. (2025) and train on 5 epochs on GSM8k-Aug-NL (the GSM8k train set augmented to 385k problems with GPT-4-generated chains, here in the variant whose CoT steps are written in natural language rather than equations, Deng et al. (2023)) plus CommonsenseQA.

Related work on CODI interp

Interpretability of latent reasoning is a quickly developing field. The following works study CODI, and are particularly relevant to this post:

  • Cywiński et al. (2025) find that on templated three-step math problems the third and fifth latent thoughts store the two intermediate values: LogitLens reads them from the residual stream at these positions, and patching the recurrent thought vectors with those of other problems changes the model's answer.
  • Dilgren and Wiegreffe (2026) find that for many problems the latents are completely unnecessary.
  • Chang et al. (2026) find that early latent vectors act as "causal hubs", and report that a trained linear mapper recovers the verbal CoT steps from the thoughts.
  • Aswal et al. (2026) find that the observational signatures (logit-lens decodability, attention patterns) also appear in control models without latent reasoning, showing that decodability does not imply causal relevance.
  • Li et al. (2026) model the latent steps as a causal graph, showing that there is an ordering to CODI's latent thoughts.

Results

Performance

We find that on the trained checkpoint, latentCoT improves over the noCoT mode, and roughly matches the verbal mode (using greedy decoding). Skipping the latent thoughts altogether drops GSM8k test accuracy from 52% to 47%. This uplift is much smaller than in the original CODI paper, where latent thoughts more than doubled GPT-2's accuracy over noCoT training (from about 19% to 44%) and roughly matched verbalCoT[2].

CODI's latent CoT is necessary on a fraction of problems. We here focus on the subset of "load-bearing" problems highlighted in red, where CODI needs its latent thoughts (it cannot solve the problem in a single pass).

Note that even within the base-needs-verbal-CoT set, CODI solves most of the tasks it gets right without any CoT (overall, about 85% of the problems solved with latent thoughts are also solved when skipping them). This is in line with the latent-unnecessity findings of Dilgren and Wiegreffe (2026).

Ablations

The advantage of latentCoT over noCoT in CODI is evidence that the latent CoT is doing something. To further analyze this, we do a series of ablations on the CoT, including removals, reorderings, foreign traces from other problems, always regenerating the later thoughts autoregressively after an intervention.

Even on load-bearing rows, ablations are not completely catastrophic. Fraction of load-bearing problems still answered correctly. Single-thought replacements are averaged over the six positions.

The fact that ablations retain some problem solving ability is surprising. This suggests that the model might not mainly do sequential autoregressive computation.

Decoding

So far, we have analyzed where the CoT is load-bearing, and manipulated parts of it through ablations. Here, we now study what the content of the latent CoT is that underlies these results.

LogitLens and J-Lens decode late layers, but not the thoughts

Cywiński et al. have used LogitLens to decode the residual stream at the thought positions. Here, we try this as well, applying both LogitLens (nostalgebraist (2020)) and J-Lens (Gurnee et al. (2026)) to both the residual stream as well as the latent thoughts at the thought positions .

Pooling the top-5 tokens over all six thought positions, both lenses read values well above chance, but only towards the output layers (see the appendix on the full LogitLens and J-lens top-5 tokens), consistent with Cywiński et al. However, the thoughts themselves stay opaque.

LogitLens (left) and J-Lens (right) fall short on the latent thoughts . On an example train problem, neither lens decodes anything from the recurrent thoughts , and the residual stream shows only the operation ("half"). Near the output, the computed intermediate 10 appears at as number words (" ten", "Ten", 十) and the answer 5 at , both at the first thought (full layerspositions grid in the appendix).

We next use more expressive interpretability techniques to study whether we can still surface problem contents.

Natural language autoencoders

Natural language autoencoders (NLAs, Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026)) autoencode activations via a natural language bottleneck. This incentivizes the bottleneck to verbalize content that helps reconstruction, in an unsupervised manner.

We here continue training of an existing Qwen3-8B NLA to verbalize the residual stream as well as the thoughts at CODI's thought positions . Alongside the reconstruction quality (FVE, fraction of variance explained) we score the pooled descriptions of all six thought positions on 60 held-out problems per checkpoint.

Verbalization performance increases with falling reconstruction loss. The readers verbalize a single vector per sample, drawn from all six thought positions in training; in the eval scans, all six positions are verbalized and scored jointly. Solid lines score containment of the gold final answer among the values mentioned in the verbalizations, dashed lines whether any gold intermediate other than the final answer is mentioned (values LLM-extracted without access to the gold). Faint horizontal lines: LogitLens and J-lens at each reader's own layer, on the same questions with the same criterion (for they are at zero).

Interestingly, we achieve much lower reconstruction error (<2% on ) than is typically reported for NLAs, yet verbalization performance stays modest for the final answer. This can be explained by a narrow task domain where the vectors are relatively low-dimensional and thus easy to reconstruct (see the appendix on thought dimensionality).

Qualitative analysis of NLA verbalizations

We then conducted an automated analysis of verbalizations over the course of training and give examples below.

Selected verbalizations by the reader (top) and the reader (bottom) of the second thought of the same problem, before (left) and after (right) reader training. Each cell is one sample at the training temperature (). In every sample, the verbalizations are genre prose, yet after training both end on the gold answer 12 as their text's "final token", while both samples write out the problem's equation after training, one with a wrong total.

Interventions

So far, we have analyzed the thought content via decoding. But before in the Ablations section we had seen that certain interventions on thoughts leave the answer correct. Here, we try to reconcile these facts by targeted interventions on the thoughts, including using the NLA.

Schema of the intervention structure. We either intervene on the latent thoughts , a given residual stream layer , or an entire residual stream column , which includes the fed thought.

Transplant-patching and

A way of doing an intervention is to consider pairs of problems whose tasks are identical, but differ in numerical values ("twin" problems, e.g. 3+6=? and 2+5=? are twins of an integer addition task). Transplanting thoughts from a donor problem should then change the computation/answer according to the donor values. We patch the original problem's thoughts into its twin's rollout and score how often the twin adopts the original's answer. We filter problems to the ones that CODI cannot solve without the latentCoT to select the subset where thoughts are load-bearing.

We patch either the thoughts alone or an entire "column" of residual stream , which transfers more of the donor CoT's state. The column includes the fed thought: is replaced together with all 36 residual streams at that position.

Transplanting thoughts between twin problems barely transplants the computation (left), while transplanting full residual stream columns considerably changes it, spread over the early thoughts (right). Unfilled bars are a skyline, i.e. the fraction of held-out problems where the NLA read of the respective fed position ( left, right) semantically matches any gold intermediate (the 1–6 tick shows the mean over the six single-position reads).

Interestingly, answer adoption is small for single positions, and considerably smaller for than for full columns, despite specifically considering load-bearing rows. Since a transplant also makes the twin lose its own answer in most cases (it keeps it in well under half of the pairs), CODI seems to require more than the latent CoT's "shape": the content matters, but cannot be transplanted via alone, presumably because the rest of the residual stream is recomputed from the twin's own question. Within , the effect comes almost entirely from the third thought: transplanting alone disrupts and transplants about as much as transplanting all six, while transplanting or has no effect at all. The third thought is also where the NLA reads intermediates best, in line with Cywiński et al. (2025), who found the third latent vector to store an intermediate value.

Intervening via the NLA

The NLA, which we previously had used for decoding, can also be used as an intervention method. To do so, we take the NLA verbalization, edit its text by replacing a numerical intermediate value with the corresponding value of the twin problem, reconstruct the activation, and patch it back into the chain-of-thought (at all six positions jointly).

Example of an NLA intervention, replacing 20 with 40. The edited verbalization then gets reconstructed via the activation reconstructor (AR), yielding z'=AR(v'), v'=edit(v), v=AV(z). Chosen is a problem where the CoT is load-bearing.

We measure then whether CODI's answer after patching the reconstructed modified activation is changed, and whether it adopts the answer that should have resulted if we indeed edited the causal path of the computation.

Editing the value in the thought's verbalization rarely implements the counterfactual. Fraction of load-bearing twin pairs that keep their own answer (gray) or adopt the counterfactual answer (blue), for (left) and (right).

For , edits disrupt the computation more than a random perturbation of the same size, but they adopt the counterfactual answer in only a handful of pairs (7%). This is, however, not far below what any transplant achieves here: reconstructing from the donor's own description adopts the donor's answer in 12% of pairs, as often as patching the donor's raw (previous section). For , the edit is not distinguishable from a random perturbation and adopts the counterfactual answer in only 2% of pairs, against 19% for the donor's description.

Conclusion

In this post, we have trained and studied a CODI model on Qwen3-8B on GSM8k data. Like previous CODIs, simple methods like LogitLens fail to decode the model's latent recurrent thoughts . However, more expressive activation verbalizers, in particular NLAs, are able to surface intermediates and answer content from the thought positions, in particular from the residual stream, though the final answer only at a modest rate.

When doing interventions, we found that the residual stream taken as a whole over layers carries computation that will guide the model to a different answer, again more so than just from the thoughts . Replacing the thoughts , raw or edited via the NLA, however induced hardly any answer adoption, even though it did disrupt the answer.

Overall, this suggests that this CODI's thoughts are 1) somewhat more opaque than the residual stream, 2) do not form a clear computational substrate as an "idealized" CoT just doing plain arithmetic on the intermediates might.

Appendix

Thought vectors are low-dimensional

We had found before that the residual stream is better decodable than the thoughts . This suggests that it is somehow richer. We here do a dimensionality analysis, showing that the residual stream indeed takes more components to explain and thus spans a higher-dimensional space across problems and positions.

Thought vectors are much more low-dimensional than the residual stream. PCA over the flattened set of vectors , .

Full LogitLens and J-lens top-5 tokens

The full LogitLens and J-Lens grids over all strided hidden states and all seven columns.

Layer-resolved J-lens and LogitLens performance

Near the output, the lenses read the answer and intermediate results well above chance, but nothing from the thoughts themselves. For each of the held-out evaluation questions of all readers, the top-k tokens of the six thought positions are pooled per layer. A problem counts if one of these tokens expresses its gold final answer (left) or an intermediate result of its reference solution (right) as a complete number, e.g. "9" or "nine". Dotted: chance, scoring the same tokens against the other questions' values. The leftmost point is the fed-back thought itself.

Composition of GSM8k test set

We here analyze whether the problems where the base model needs verbal CoT coincide with the problem that CODI can do only with verbal or latent CoT.

Venn diagram of different GSM8k test set subsets. Base needs CoT means the base model fails the single pass but solves with verbal CoT. CODI needs some CoT means its noCoT decode fails but the latent or the verbal mode solves the problem.

Activation oracles

In the main text, we have used natural language autoencoders to analyze CODI's thoughts. Here, we use activation oracles (Karvonen et al. (2025)). In contrast to NLAs, they are trained in a supervised manner, instead of a pure reconstruction signal. Thus, they may perhaps have higher recall, at the cost of some inductive bias.

What should be the supervision signal, given that we don't know the content of the thoughts? We approach this by imputing the thought content. Specifically, training goes as follows: each training sample draws a random set of vectors to verbalize: sources from the band plus the thoughts , at a random subset of thought positions , ordered. To have a baseline, a tenth of the samples feed question-region residual stream activations alone, and another tenth feed them together with the thoughts. Independently, 60 percent of the samples feed activations only, 20 percent replace them with the teacher transcript as plain text, and 20 percent feed both. We then ask one of eight questions about the computation (the final answer, single or all intermediate values, single or all step sentences, the operations used, the step count, or the numbers given in the problem) and supervise on the corresponding ground-truth completion, written either as sentences ("The discount is 20/100 * $60 = $12. So the game will cost $60 - $12 = $48.") or as bare values ("12, 48"). We finetune this model from the plain Qwen3-8B base with a fresh LoRA, otherwise the architecture is the same as the NLA's.

Activation oracle training increases accuracy on held-out problems. Solid lines score first-number answer accuracy, and dashed lines the judged any-intermediate match as in the NLA figure. Faint horizontal lines: LogitLens and J-lens on the same streams and questions (for they are at zero). The appendix on eval scaling curves shows the full curves with the val CE panel.

Importantly, for the final answer, the full and the -only reads are above the question-token only baseline (for intermediates, however, the question-only read does at least as well as the thought reads, so the oracle may recompute intermediates from the question rather than read them from the thoughts). As for the NLA, adding to helps for the final answer, though part of this may come from layers 35 and 36, where the lenses alone already read the answer for a third of problems.

Readouts by the activation oracle of a showcase problem, before (left) and after (right) reader training. Each cell shows two samples at under our italic one-line digest. At the final checkpoint both reads recover the answer-feeding intermediate in every sample; the full read (top) gives the gold answer in one of the two samples, while the -only read (bottom) lands near but off it.

Scaling

The NLA figure in the main text and the activation-oracle figure in the activation-oracle appendix omit their middle panel for compactness. Here we show the full three-panel versions, generated from the same scripts and data passes as the compact ones. The middle panels render the eval error on double-log axes shared with the train panel, so the eval scaling can be compared against the training curve directly.

NLA scaling curves. As the main-text figure, plus the middle panel showing the decode error (one minus the decode score) on the train panel's double-log axes, and dotted lines showing the coincidence control (the any-intermediate criterion for verbalizations of an unrelated problem's thoughts). Both readers exceed the coincidence floor throughout training.

Activation oracle scaling curves. As the figure in the AO section, plus the middle panel showing transformed eval accuracy on a log-scale.

Reusing vs regenerating later thoughts

Whether the later thoughts are reused or regenerated changes little. Fraction of the 104 load-bearing problems still answered correctly when one thought is replaced, either reusing the recorded later thoughts or regenerating them autoregressively from the corrupted thought.

    Note that the different modes trained jointly into a single model imposes an expressivity constraint: a model trained with verbalCoT SFT alone reaches much better performance. Still, within the class of jointly trained models, the latent over noCoT uplift is an interesting phenomenon to study.
